summary: Small, hardy, always-hungry wrasse found around nearly every wharf, breakwater, and rocky structure in NB/NS/PEI — the easiest, most reliable species in this guide and a great confidence-builder or between-bites distraction.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
Cunner (*Tautogolabrus adspersus*), locally called bergall, conner, or chogset, are small members of the wrasse family (Labridae) — the same family as tautog/blackfish further south. They range from the Gulf of St. Lawrence and Newfoundland down to Chesapeake Bay, making the NB/NS/PEI coast core habitat, not the edge of their range. Juveniles show a black circular spot on the rear dorsal fin; larger adults develop gold flecks along the sides. Colour is variable and mottled, blending in well against rocks and pilings.

Cunner are non-migratory, structure-oriented fish, typically found from the shallows down to over 100 m, but around wharves and breakwaters they're usually right up near the pilings and rocks within easy casting range. One unusual trait: cunner survive winter by going into a dormant, torpid state, wedging into rock crevices and barely moving once water temperatures drop below roughly 5°C — which is why they disappear from the fishery in the cold months and reappear reliably every spring.

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md: Cunner fish well through the open-water season, roughly spring through fall, once water has warmed past their winter torpor threshold. There's no tight seasonal window like a spawning run — this is a consistent, any-warm-day fishery, which is part of why it's a good option to fall back on when a target species (mackerel, striped bass) isn't cooperating. Any time of day works; they're not particularly tide- or light-dependent compared to species like mackerel or striped bass.

sources.label: Canadian Journal of Zoology, Winter habits of the cunner, Tautogolabrus adspersus, in Newfoundland

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
Cunner relate to hard structure almost exclusively: wharf pilings, breakwaters, rock jetties, bridge abutments, and shipwrecks.

- **NB:** Shediac Harbour is specifically noted as good cunner water; the Cocagne Cape Marina breakwater and any Northumberland Strait wharf with pilings will hold fish.
- **NS:** **Halifax Harbour** and the Northwest Arm are well-documented cunner water right off the downtown waterfront docks; expect them anywhere along the Atlantic coast, Bay of Fundy, and Cape Breton with wharf or rock structure — this is one of the most evenly distributed species in the province.
- **PEI:** Georgetown's waterfront and other Three Rivers-area wharves are a good bet, as is any structure around Boughton Bay/Panmure Island.

Because cunner relate so tightly to structure everywhere, virtually any public wharf or breakwater in all three provinces is worth a look.

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Rod | Light spinning rod, any you have on hand — no specialized gear needed. |
| Hooks | Small bait hooks (size 6-10) — cunner have small mouths and are notorious bait-stealers on oversized hooks. |
| Bait | Clam strips or worms are the standard, most-recommended baits. |
| Rig | Simple small bait rig or a plain hook with a split shot — no finesse required. |

sources.label: NorEast Fishing Forum, Tips on Bergall (cunner) fishing

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body_md:
1. Find any wharf, breakwater, or rocky jetty with visible pilings, rockpiles, or bridge abutments.
2. Drop a small baited hook straight down beside the structure — no need to cast far or work a retrieve.
3. Cunner will take almost any small bait or lure presented near their cover, so this is a genuinely no-technique fishery — perfect for kids or beginners.
4. Expect fast, aggressive bites and a fair number of stolen baits; re-bait often rather than waiting out slow bites, since cunner are opportunistic and quick.
5. If bigger-fish tactics (striped bass, mackerel) are slow, dropping a small rig for cunner nearby is a reliable way to keep rods bent while you wait.

sources.label: NorEast Fishing Forum, Tips on Bergall (cunner) fishing

sections.heading: Handling & Table Notes
sections.body_md: Cunner are hardy and easy to handle — a light grip and standard hook removal is all that's needed. They're an underrated eating fish: firm, mild white flesh, though small size means more cleaning effort per meal than a larger species. Most anglers targeting bigger species treat cunner as an incidental catch-and-release bonus rather than table fare, but there's nothing wrong with keeping a few for a fish fry if you're catching them anyway.

sections.heading: Conservation Notes
sections.body_md: No at-risk status or specific conservation concern turned up for cunner in this research — they're an abundant, resilient, non-migratory species. No dedicated recreational bag limit turned up in current DFO Gulf Region or Maritimes Region notices; fish them as a light, sustainable, any-size fishery.

variants.name: Tautog (Blackfish)
variants.how_to_tell: Tautog is a much bigger, heavier-bodied fish, averaging 1-3 lb and reaching up to 3 ft/25 lb versus cunner's small size throughout life. Tautog has a high-arched, steep, rounded head profile with a blunt snout and thick rubbery lips, while cunner has a more pointed head profile and thinner lips. Tautog's dark, mottled blackish-brown coloring also runs heavier and less speckled than cunner's variable mottled pattern with gold flecking.
variants.where_found: Same structure cunner relates to — wharf pilings, breakwaters, rock jetties — with tautog present at the northern edge of its range in Nova Scotia, overlapping cunner water.
variants.notes: No regulatory concern in this region, but worth knowing a noticeably larger, blunt-headed wrasse on the same light gear is likely a tautog, not an oversized cunner.

variants.name: Juvenile Pollock
variants.how_to_tell: Juvenile ("harbor") pollock share the same wharf-piling and breakwater structure as cunner and are a similar size in their first year or two, but pollock has a forked tail (cunner's is rounded/fan-shaped), a single soft dorsal fin running the length of the back with no spiny section (cunner's dorsal fin has a distinct spiny front section), and a cod-family body shape versus cunner's deeper-bodied wrasse shape.
variants.where_found: Both hold tight to the same inshore wharf and breakwater structure region-wide, especially in summer and fall.
variants.notes: No regulatory concern, but useful when a mixed bag of small structure-oriented fish comes up and includes something that doesn't quite look like a cunner.
